articles.headline: What can schools offer to students?
articles.author: S

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
When I was in junior high school in Japan, I spent most of the time studying or participating in the school's sports club. I used to wake up at 5 am and come back home at 9 pm. Being trapped at school for more than 12 hours a day felt like I was a prisoner. But it definitely taught me good lessons that helped shape me as a good member of society. 

During my time as a student, my teachers taught me not only how to be academically intelligent, but also how to develop socialisation. 

I think that the ultimate goal of school is to make its students successful members of society, and school is not a monolithic entity. It offers students many ways to contribute to society, through personal growth, academic achievement, social care, and economic contribution. Balancing these different metrics and offering different opportunities, and playing as a safety net for children is the purpose of schools. 

The 2023 study by Toraman and Korkmaz frames the meaning of school through two different components by surveying more than 6,000 school students across Turkey. The concepts of educare and educere come from Latin roots, and these philosophies represent how school is meant to exist. 

Educare is a functionalist approach, meaning that the basis of this method is preserving  and focusing on existing social systems. This promotes the idea that students should be successful by becoming rote learners and following the paths that their parents have already paved. In practice, this comes with a diploma, certificate or tertiary degree so that students can compete in professional settings. 

In contrast, the educere focuses more on individual growth and creativity. It promotes the opposite of the educare philosophy, and it creates new generations that are equipped with questions, imagination, and innovative solutions for issues and problems that have not been solved yet. Under his concept, a student should spend more time on internal development, discovering new things, paving the way for new paths that nobody has imagined before. 

I argue that these two concepts can fulfil what school can ultimately achieve. Through educare, students develop skills and abilities with which they can compete in an existing system, generating benefits to humankind and society. Simultaneously, through educere, students develop into the individuals that they seek to be by shaping their character and gaining knowledge. And as a byproduct of these journeys, they can acquire transferable skills that further strengthen their success in professional settings or their adult lives. 

Balance is important. Teachers or parents cannot fully predict in what way their students or children will become successful, so they have to take a long-term approach to risk management. Fostering both social development and individual development can at least help them reduce risks, such as demoralisation, disengagement, disrespect, or narrow perspectives. 

Schools prevent social isolation. Students can view their classroom as a place to become a member of a community, where they can develop a sense of belonging and responsibility. These are core qualities and soft skills that are necessary to help students transition from childhood to adulthood. 

This also leads to the idea that school acts as a safety net for future generations. Students who come from lower-income families or lower parental education levels can view schools as a pragmatic path for them to escape financial struggles and eventually secure a high-quality job. In this case, school offers a spotlight to children who come from disadvantaged backgrounds. 

Therefore, schools exist to make future generations good members of society. They offer opportunities to become academic, emotionally intelligent, fit into society, develop their characteristics, or offer a safety net so that students can reduce risks that might cause unproductive and disengaging behaviours.

articles.headline: Who should decide what students learn at school?
articles.author: S

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
Imagine two students of the same age living ten kilometres apart. One teacher decides that financial literacy and AI should dominate the classroom; another believes classical literature and history deserve most of the year. Should something as important as a child's education depend largely on which teacher happens to stand in front of them? 

The core knowledge and learning outcomes are critical to student life. I argue that public curriculum authorities should decide what those core knowledge and learning outcomes criteria should be. On the contrary, individual schools and teachers ought to have direction over teaching methods and some options for textbooks and teaching materials. 

First, consistency and equality matter. Students should not receive radically different foundational knowledge solely because they attend different schools, come from different socioeconomic backgrounds, or have parents with varying levels of influence. 

Rather, the government curriculum system can provide a common baseline which allows schools to choose suitable resources according to budget, student ability, and local circumstances. 

Second, if teachers decide what students can read and learn, they could bring their own ideologies, biases, and preferences into classrooms. Although this doesn’t necessarily mean that they deliberately indoctrinate students, this system can possibly give agency to teachers where they can determine what standards students should have. 

A centralised system is necessary when formulating and structuring learning materials. In Japan, for example, the Ministry of Education is responsible for the nation’s school system from kindergarten to universities. This includes setting national guidelines, a textbook screening system, and teacher licensing. 

Under the supervision of Japan’s Ministry of Education, the guidelines dictate the precise number of hours students should commit to in the classroom annually, and they require specific numbers for each subject, such as mathematics, Japanese, English, and moral education at every grade level. 

Third, education is not only an individual experience; it is also a collective responsibility. 

If decisions about what students learn are spread too widely across individual teachers, parents, and schools, responsibility can become fragmented. This creates a basic problem: if students leave school without essential knowledge, who is ultimately accountable? 

A common curriculum helps establish a shared foundation in areas such as literacy, numeracy, science, history and civic understanding. It also gives students, regardless of which school they attend, access to a broadly consistent educational baseline. 

Teachers and schools should still have flexibility in how they deliver these subjects, but the core learning expectations should remain publicly defined. Without that shared framework, education risks becoming too dependent on local preferences rather than a common set of responsibilities toward the next generation. 

In contrast, there is a benefit of allowing teachers to decide what students can read and learn, which is flexibility. Teachers interact with students every day, and they are also aware of which materials are outdated, which topics are no longer to be taught, and which new skills are important for future generations. For example, financial literacy, AI ethics and literacy, and data visualisation skills are core qualities that companies look for regardless of industry. 

With flexibility, teachers may be able to adapt lessons to follow the rapidly changing world much faster than a government curriculum because the process requires a number of approvals. 

However, speed and flexibility should not come at the cost of consistency and accountability. If every teacher can independently decide what is important, students may receive very different educational foundations depending on their school or teacher. 

A better approach is for public education authorities to define the core knowledge and learning outcomes, while teachers retain freedom over the materials, examples, and teaching methods they use to achieve them. 

What students learn should not depend entirely on the preferences of individual teachers, parents or schools. Education shapes the knowledge, values and skills that future generations carry into society, so there needs to be a clear and publicly accountable framework. 

Governments and education authorities should define the core curriculum, while teachers should retain flexibility in how they teach it. This balance protects consistency and accountability without removing professional judgement from the classroom. The goal should not be total control, but a shared direction for every student.

articles.headline: Compulsory Immunisation Is How We Prepare for the Next Pandemic
articles.author: K

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
A University in Texas suggests that the real death toll of Covid 19 is close to 21.2 million people. That is almost the number of people who reside in Australia – and that number does not include cases of Long Covid which can also shorten life expectancy and therefore increase those mortality statistics. So the fact that most of our large workplaces and education facilities currently have no real precautionary practices in place for any kind of pandemic risk is both irresponsible and alarming. By treating the existence of viruses and infections like COVID-19, SARS or even monkeypox as something that is now just part of ordinary daily life, we are becoming way too complacent about the possibilities of another pandemic. The idea that we can now just be vaccinated against Covid or the yearly flu has allowed us to forgot about the contagious nature of those kinds of illnesses and their ability to spread quickly and exponentially. We are now falling asleep at the wheel.

Recent scientific data suggests that even if you have had the Covid 19 vaccine, unless you get a booster shot every 6 months or so, and even then I’m not talking about those targeted at the new strains of the infection, you are still going to be losing something like approximately half of your defensive antibodies every 108 days or so. That means that if the jab gave you 90% protection in the beginning, after 6 months it would only be around 70% and without another dose of the vaccine it would just continue to wane. That means that in the last say 3-4 years most of us who were immunised during the pandemic are losing our ability to fight off Covid, as well as any other strain of the SARS virus. That is why bigger institutions and workplaces who have a large number of employees or who teach a large number of young people, must have safeguards and precautions put in place in case this kind of event happens again. 

I believe the most important piece of this puzzle is the need for employers at any largescale company or school to adopt the policy of compulsory immunisation. Yes – people want bodily autonomy but they can choose to not work there. And yes – people would have to prove that they were maintaining the number of boosters required to achieve sufficient herd immunity -  but this is the foundation needed for us to be better equipped to deal with another outbreak of Covid or something similar. 

I can understand that people don’t want to be told what to do, that they want choice, but is that enough to want to risk another lockdown? Another million people gone? I do not want to watch another family suffer the way mine did when my grandfather got sick and we could only wave him off to what would be his eventual his death through a clear glass window. Of course the only way to maintain this kind of precaution would be to also require the use of masks for those visiting the school or workplace but isn’t that a sacrifice we should be willing to make? If we could ensure that we don’t see another outbreak of the Corona virus would it not be a worthwhile enterprise? When I think back to those lockdown days where I spent hours watching news reports of more people getting sick, more people dying and I remember how terrifying it was, I still get a knot in my stomach and my throat closes up. If I had known that by keeping up with being vaccinated and wearing protection when I engaged with people I could prevent that situation from happening again – I would gladly be poked with a needle once every 6 months and flash my immunisation status to whomever wanted to see it.

We need to start preparing ourselves now because Covid 19 shook the very foundations of how we live, work and interact with each other. Rather than viewing the virus as just another inconvenience that our global existence has to consider, we need to remember the disruption and destruction it wrought upon us. Workplaces and educational institutions must develop better infrastructure in order to be prepared for the next Covid pandemic and that means compulsory immunisation. Get out there and get your booster shot so that we never have to live a ‘lockdown life’ again.

articles.headline: Luck Is Not a Public Health Strategy
articles.author: K

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
A government's first responsibility is to protect its people. That principle lies at the heart of the social contract between citizens and the state. We elect representatives with the expectation that they will make decisions in the public interest, particularly when our safety and wellbeing are under threat. Yet when it comes to preparing for the next pandemic, Australians have every reason to ask an uncomfortable question: have our leaders truly learned the lessons of COVID-19, or have they simply moved on?

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed both strengths and weaknesses in Australia's response to a public health emergency. While some decisions undoubtedly saved lives, the overall response was often slow, inconsistent and, in many cases, devastating for families, businesses and healthcare workers. Thousands of Australians lost their lives, countless more experienced long-term health complications, and communities endured years of uncertainty. Those events should have prompted an enduring national conversation about preparedness. Instead, the discussion has largely disappeared.

That silence is troubling.

Pandemics are not once-in-a-century anomalies. Infectious disease experts have repeatedly warned that another global outbreak is not a matter of if, but when. COVID-19 may have faded from daily headlines, but viruses have not stopped evolving simply because the public has grown weary of hearing about them. SARS-related viruses continue to circulate, influenza remains a constant global threat, and diseases such as Ebola and mpox demonstrate how quickly outbreaks can emerge and spread in an increasingly connected world. Ignoring these realities does not reduce the risk; it merely leaves us more vulnerable when the next crisis arrives.

The question Australians should be asking is simple: what has changed since 2020?

Have governments developed faster response plans? Are hospitals better equipped to cope with a sudden surge in patients? Are vaccine distribution strategies more efficient? Has communication between federal and state governments improved? Most importantly, are these plans publicly available so that Australians can have confidence in the systems designed to protect them?These should not be controversial questions. They are reasonable expectations in any modern democracy.

To be fair, inquiries were conducted into Australia's handling of COVID-19, and numerous reports examined both the public health response and the enormous economic consequences of the pandemic. Yet reports alone do not guarantee meaningful reform. Recommendations only matter if governments act on them and continue to review them as circumstances change. Unfortunately, pandemic preparedness no longer appears to occupy much space in our national conversation. It rarely features prominently during election campaigns. Parliamentary debate focuses on the issues dominating today's news cycle, while planning for future health emergencies receives comparatively little public attention. That may make political sense, but it is not responsible governance.

Many Australians simply assume that governments have comprehensive plans ready to be activated if another dangerous virus emerges. Perhaps they do. But assumptions are not the same as transparency. Unless you work within the healthcare system or are directly involved in government planning, it is difficult to know what procedures currently exist or whether they have been updated to reflect the hard lessons of COVID-19. Every government, regardless of political persuasion, has a duty to ensure Australia is prepared for future health emergencies. Likewise, every opposition has a responsibility to scrutinise those preparations rather than waiting until the next crisis exposes their shortcomings. Public health should never become collateral damage in political point-scoring.

Democracies function best when voters ask difficult questions rather than assuming someone else already has the answers. We should expect our Health Minister, health departments and leading medical organisations to explain what has been learned since COVID-19 and what practical measures are now in place. The end of mandatory COVID-19 vaccinations and restrictions may have signalled a return to normal life, but it should not have marked the end of pandemic planning. Complacency is a dangerous substitute for preparedness. 

Australia has often been called the lucky country. But luck is not a public health strategy. We cannot afford to rely on hope or assume that future outbreaks will somehow be less severe than COVID-19. The true measure of responsible leadership is not how governments respond once disaster strikes, but how thoroughly they prepare before it does.

If the next pandemic arrives tomorrow, Australians deserve the confidence of knowing their leaders have been planning for it today.

articles.headline: How Platforms Trap Us in the Attention Economy
articles.author: R

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
It's been well over a decade since the popularity of platforms being integrated in our population across the globe. If asking for someone's phone number as a way to keep in touch was a norm back in the early 2000s, then the more common courtesy now is to ask for their social media account, you'll most likely understand that it's a norm to exist on these platforms. Given such context, platform usage is not much of a novelty, much as the same with the conversation about its design and the facilitated habits that comes with. Especially for the case of compulsive scrolling, or some would describe it as 'doomscrolling', the endless feed opens up a critical debate on the problems of cognitive dysfunction and our attention fragmentation, with this technology while posing the important question – who should be responsible for it?

I'm a part of a generation who's exposed to social media platforms at a young age, my first ever Facebook account was created when I was 12. No one really taught me how to use it, the only goal back then was to play games and chat with other kids/strangers online about whatever topics it might be. Fast forward to 2026, the landscape hasn't been the same, I've now become an adult and the platforms I once knew also changed. There is a slight awareness within my cohort on how our relationship with the feed: Who do we follow? Does the algorithm affect our mood? How much control do we have on the screen and its buttons? But one common thread that we're somewhat aware of is the amount of time we've been spending on platforms as a hybrid option of both entertainment and personal connections. We start to wonder how come we can spend the entire evening just scrolling (while beating ourselves up that we can do much better than this). Afterall, a large part of being an adult is the ability to have some modicum of autonomy, especially for something supposedly as trivial as picking up our phones for a scroll. However, it appears to be much more complicated when it comes to the ability to control our habits, and some start to wonder whether these platforms' designs and its creators are the real culprit, or how philosophy would put it, is there truly free will or it's the universe's doing?

In this case, 'the universe' can be understood as platforms, and us mere users are its subjects. Of course, no platform is the same, and the robust digital markets do offer us several poisons to pick from. But for the more prominent choices like Facebook, Instagram, Tiktok, or the likes of it – The endless scroll is an integral part of how they trap us, to serve up the purpose of The Attention Economy. The intentional introduction of the endless scroll is known to capture users' retention and serve the purpose of getting users to engage with commercial activities via advertisement links, sponsored content. It's now become an industry that generates so much commercial activities, making the internet to be no longer the carefree social space like how it once was. Hence, the matter of platform design, or in this case, the endless scroll, becomes an ethical responsibility for platform companies to protect its users/consumers in this digital market.

Given the scale that platforms have become, it's hard to ignore the effects that it's brought to the population. Much like many other aspects in our social life: from education, labour, and many forms of consumption. Our participation within platforms only has a certain degree of choices and autonomy, while the much bigger issues of platform rules and designs would lie in the hands of the companies behind them. While it's possible that an individual can try to be active in their digital habit by finding ways to regulate their scrolling behavior, the responsibility for platforms to facilitate a better feature for its users is equally crucial, if not, even more critical.

articles.headline: Should We Slow Down AI Development?
articles.author: R

attention_check.text: What was the main topic of this article?

articles.body:
The framing of Artificial intelligence (AI) or Large Language Models (LLMs) discourse on its development and potential threat can be understood through some of the main factors: Geopolitics and national security, economic competition, and environmental sustainability. Given how AI technology for the most part is owned by private corporations, its scale and impact have made government officials step in and balance between regulations and business practices. The issue comes into two folds: To develop AI for its economic and security potentials, or to slow down this process considering the risks that follow.

For one, AI technology and its data is considered a great asset for surveillance and military intel. NATO's revised AI strategy explicitly identifies both the opportunities and risks of military AI, while committing the Alliance to accelerate responsible adoption and protect against adversarial uses of the technology. The United States has adopted a similarly competitive approach: its June 2026 National Security Presidential Memorandum directs the national-security establishment to accelerate AI adoption, adapt commercial and open-source models for military purposes, and expand high-security computing infrastructure. This is not without the fact that the biggest players of this technology come from the US itself, where its domestic policies can affect the entire global outreach of these AI companies' products such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In an already US-tech reliant world, and also with its military power, it's evidently beneficial and predictable for the US to keep up with this advantage. Hence, making it the leading trendsetter for other regions to follow with the race.

In the most basic sense, the rise of AI is not without an infrastructure that supports its expansion and what's required for this tool to come into form. Semiconductor manufacturers, data-centre operators, cloud providers, networking companies and energy suppliers are experiencing significant increases in demand. For instance, The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that global data-centre electricity consumption could more than double to approximately 945 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030, with AI identified as the principal driver of this growth. This growing electricity requirement creates a direct connection between AI development and climate policy. The IEA estimates that coal currently supplies approximately 30% of electricity consumed by data centres globally, while renewables supply around 27%, natural gas 26% and nuclear power 15%. Additionally, there is also a human cost in training these AI models, where reports of poor working conditions for AI annotations have been occurring in places in East Africa, India, the Philippines, and even refugees living in Kenya’s Dadaab and Lebanon’s Shatila. This opens up a debate on whether this expansion is justifiable given the sufferings it's creating.

It's fairly evident on the human and environmental cost to sustain this technology, and the eerie parallel it has with colonialism via violence and extraction of resources with its given pace. Some would raise predictions to how AI is meant to design and integrate in our daily lives when it comes to our jobs, relationships, and overall human activities. AI/LLMs in its more useful form has long been a tool for large-scale content moderation that has been used for social media platforms, making it easier to filter through the sea of content that can be customised to users, while offloading a substantial amount of work for a human moderator. On the other hand, there would some concerning effects of generative AI, where it has been the main catalyst for the rise of online scamming, revenge porn/sexual harassment, and causing a wave of controversies within the creative industry. What might determine the future of this technology remains in the direction of much bigger stakeholders, like corporations and governments around the globe.

Ultimately, AI represents a convergence of three global competitions: political-economical power, national security and environmental sustainability. Governments are unlikely to abandon AI development because the economic and strategic costs of falling behind competitors may be considerable. The countries that succeed in the coming decades may not simply be those that develop the most powerful AI, but those capable of combining advanced computing, secure energy supplies, economic competitiveness and credible climate policy. The central challenge is ensuring that the race for AI leadership does not undermine the environmental and geopolitical stability that governments ultimately seek to protect.
